content: Palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia (PPE), also known as hand-foot syndrome, is a dermatologic condition primarily affecting the palms of the hands and soles of the feet. It is most commonly associated with the use of certain chemotherapeutic agents in cancer treatment. The condition manifests as a painful, tingling, and erythematous reaction that progresses to well-demarcated swelling and plaques, often followed by a desquamative phase during resolution. PPE is classified into four grades based on the severity of symptoms and toxicity. The pathophysiology of PPE remains under investigation, but proposed mechanisms include rapid cell turnover in the palms and soles, gravitational forces, unique vascular anatomy in these areas, and temperature gradients. Additionally, high drug concentrations in eccrine sweat glands, particularly in the palms and soles, contribute to the condition. In cases associated with pegylated liposomal doxorubicin (PLD), the drug is deposited in sweat and subsequently smeared onto the skin surface, infiltrating the stratum corneum, which acts as a reservoir for the drug and leads to the characteristic symptoms. Histologically, PPE is characterized by nonspecific features such as vacuolar degeneration of the basal cell layer, mild spongiosis, keratinocyte necrosis, papillary dermal edema, lymphocytic infiltrates, and partial separation of the epidermis from the dermis. Perivascular infiltrates composed of eosinophils and lymphocytes may also be observed. In some cases, eccrine squamous syringometaplasia or neutrophilic eccrine hidradenitis may be present. Emerging evidence suggests that small-fiber neuropathy may contribute to the pain and dysesthesia experienced by patients. PPE is most frequently associated with chemotherapeutic agents such as pegylated liposomal doxorubicin, 5-fluorouracil, and cytarabine. Other agents, including methotrexate (even at low doses), mitotane, docetaxel, capecitabine, vinorelbine, gemcitabine, and sorafenib, have also been implicated. Risk factors for PPE include prolonged exposure to chemotherapeutic drugs, continuous intravenous infusion, daily oral administration, and liposomal encapsulation of drugs, which prolong their half-life. Cooling mechanisms, higher numbers of PLD cycles, and the presence of mucositis, neutropenia, or peripheral neuropathy may predict the development of PPE. Differentiating PPE from other conditions is critical. For example, tinea manuum, a fungal infection, responds to antifungal therapy and must be ruled out. Acute graft-versus-host disease, commonly seen in bone marrow transplant recipients, can mimic PPE but typically involves other body regions. Hand-foot skin reactions due to tyrosine kinase inhibitors may also resemble PPE but present with focal hyperkeratotic lesions rather than diffuse erythema. The natural history of PPE begins with numbness or tingling in the palms and soles, progressing to painful, symmetric swelling and erythematous plaques. Desquamation follows during resolution. A notable complication of PPE is the loss of fingerprints, as documented in a patient treated with capecitabine who faced challenges during airport security screening. Diagnosis of PPE in cancer patients receiving chemotherapy is primarily clinical, based on the characteristic painful swelling of the hands and feet. A thorough history and physical examination are essential to exclude differential diagnoses. Preventive strategies include the use of atorvastatin and polyprenol combinations, as well as antioxidant-rich ointments with high radical protection factors. Dose reduction of PLD to less than 10 mg/m² weekly has been shown to effectively prevent PPE. Supportive measures, patient education, and expert guidance are critical for managing and preventing PPE, given the limited literature on the condition.
